displayQuote: There is a certain relief in change, even though it be from bad to worse

meta.title: Who really said "There is a certain relief in change, even though it be from bad to worse"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Washington Irving wrote it, in the 1824 preface to Tales of a Traveller. The famous line is genuine, just usually cut short of its stage-coach punchline.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is a certain relief in change, even though it be from bad to worse'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Washington Irving, from his 1824 preface to Tales of a Traveller. Verified against the original edition — and the line is usually quoted only halfway.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in Irving’s own preface, “To the Reader,” opening his 1824 collection Tales of a Traveller. The full sentence runs on with a stage-coach joke — the short line circulating online is a genuine (if truncated) quotation.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: There is a certain relief in change, even though it be from bad to worse! As I have often found in travelling in a stage-coach, that it is often a comfort to shift one’s position, and be bruised in a new place.
trail: The line is listed in the sourced (not disputed) section of Wikiquote’s Washington Irving page ↗, cited to Tales of a Traveller (1824), Preface.
The exact wording, including the stage-coach continuation, appears in a scanned original edition on the Internet Archive ↗.
Popular quote sites reproduce the line under Irving’s name, some truncating it and a few dropping the article as “There is certain relief in change,” per Goodreads ↗.
source.excerptNote: Irving’s own preface, using the discomforts of stage-coach travel as a metaphor for the shifting variety of tales in the collection. The popular quotation stops at “bad to worse,” dropping the joke that gives it its point.
source.rightsNote: Tales of a Traveller was first published in 1824, well before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff, so both the work and this line are in the public domain.

author.name: Washington Irving
author.heading: About Washington Irving
author.bio: Washington Irving was one of the first American writers to win international fame, best known for the stories “Rip Van Winkle” and “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow.” He published Tales of a Traveller in 1824 under his pen name Geoffrey Crayon, framing its stories with a wry, self-deprecating preface addressed “To the Reader.” His genial, ironic voice made lines like this one quotable long after the book itself faded from popularity.

misattribution.heading: A note on how it’s quoted
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Washington Irving is correct — this is genuinely his. The only distortion is in how the line travels.

items.why: The widely shared form stops at “even though it be from bad to worse,” dropping Irving’s stage-coach punchline — “that it is often a comfort to shift one’s position, and be bruised in a new place” — which is where the humour and the metaphor actually land, per the original preface ↗.
A few quote sites drop the article and render it “There is certain relief in change”; the original preface reads “There is a certain relief in change,” as shown on Wikiquote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: rightly credited to Washington Irving and drawn from his 1824 preface — just usually quoted only halfway, per Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Read as a standalone aphorism, the line sounds almost stoic — a case that any change, even for the worse, brings a kind of relief simply by breaking the monotony of a bad situation. That is why it circulates today among quotes about change and resilience.

In context it is lighter than that. Irving offers it half in jest, comparing the shifting variety of his tales to the small mercy of changing one’s cramped posture in a jolting stage-coach — trading one ache for a fresh one. The wisdom is real, but Irving delivers it with a shrug.
detailsBody: Tales of a Traveller (1824) appeared under Irving’s pen name Geoffrey Crayon and was coolly received at the time, though it is now valued for stories like “The Devil and Tom Walker.” The self-mocking preface “To the Reader” is where this line lives.
context.pull: A comfort to shift one’s position, and be bruised in a new place.
